items.question: What mistakes do pastors usually make that hurt their ministry?
items.book: The Top Ten Mistakes that Pastors Make
items.text:
Friend, our books name several mistakes pastors make that wound their own ministry. Choosing to bear little fruit is one of them — leaving a fruitful place for somewhere with no one to preach to, when God is glorified by much fruit, as John 15:8 says [1]. Turning into a Pharisee is another, loving the chief seats and greetings in the markets, as Matthew 23:6-7 describes [2]. Wrong priorities kill a ministry too — chasing invitations and honorariums while never building your own church, or giving priority to the rich and powerful while setting aside the young and the poor [4].

There is also being slow about ministry, slow to obey the call of God, when speed matters greatly [7]; and downplaying humility, refusing to become as little children, as Matthew 18:3 says, so that a pastor can no longer be taught [8]. Disappointing shepherds choose their own sacrifices instead of obeying, stop seeing themselves as sheep who still need leading, and fail to remain small in their own eyes, as 1 Samuel 15:16-17 shows with Saul [3]. And pride, when it infects a man, brings an overconfidence like Korah's, who overstepped his bounds against Moses [6].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapters 1, 3, 7, 8 and 9 of *The Top Ten Mistakes that Pastors Make*, chapter 31 of *The Art of Shepherding* and chapter 2 of *Not A Novice*.

Scriptures referenced: 1 Samuel 15:16-17; Matthew 18:3; Matthew 23:6-7; John 7:6; John 15:8.

items.question: What should I do when one of them is a leader I trained?
items.text:
When a leader you trained breaks away, the books speak plainly. There is nothing wrong with starting your own ministry, but there is something wrong when a person sets himself up as an alternative to the congregation he used to pastor, thereby destroying it — building up one congregation while subtly destroying another [1]. That is what happened with the pilot you trained: an independent spirit took over, he started a church near the one he had led, and others followed his example until the city was dotted with splinter churches and confused members [1].

The counsel is to remove disloyal people quickly. If someone indicates his desire to leave, it is best for him not to stay on but to leave immediately, because his heart has already left; the extra months are not worth the trouble they yield, for "a little leaven leaveneth the whole lump" (1 Corinthians 5:6), and after Judas resigned Jesus told him, "That thou doest, do quickly" (John 13:27) [6]. People who don't want to be with you must go, and as soon as possible [6].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 5 of *Those who leave you* and chapter 3 of *Loyalty and Disloyalty*.

Scriptures referenced: John 13:27; 1 Corinthians 5:6.

items.question: How do I start a new church in a town where we have no members?
items.text:
Begin by counting the cost, because it will not be easy and not many people want to identify with a small thing [5]. You do not need a crowd to start: where two or three are gathered in His name, there He is in the midst of them (Matthew 18:20), and the Lighthouse Cathedral was started with as few as five people [6]. If you are truly called of God, the only person you need is yourself [6].

Start in an honourable way, through witnessing, following up converts, and gathering sheep together, without breaking up someone else's church [5]. The basics are praying, witnessing and following up converts [6]. Do not be financially desperate in these early stages; find a job and start the church as a lay person, so that people see you are not ministering for financial gain [1][2]. Do not be discouraged by fluctuating attendance, for that is how sheep behave [3][4].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 7 of *The Mega Church* and chapter 20 of *Church Planting*.

Scriptures referenced: Matthew 18:20; Luke 14:28.

items.question: What is true forgiveness?
items.text:
True forgiveness is releasing all hurts, bitterness, and wickedness from your heart, so that Satan finds a closed door to your heart and a horde of demons is denied access [7]. It means dismissing the thorny, painful issues, giving up all claims against the one who offended you, cancelling any indebtedness, making no more mention of the matter, stopping resentment and anger, and cancelling any punishments you had planned [7]. As Ephesians 4:32 says, we are to be kind and tenderhearted, forgiving one another even as God for Christ's sake has forgiven us [7].

A real test of forgiveness is being able to pray sincerely for the well-being of the one who hurt you, and to walk in love and pray for your offenders, as Jesus taught [1][7]. Forgiveness also means leaving vengeance to God rather than taking it up yourself, since He says, "Vengeance is mine" (Romans 12:19), and He has a repayment plan for those who harm you [3][5].

items.question: People are spreading lies about me in the church. How should I respond?
items.text:
I'm sorry you're carrying this. Our books speak directly to slander, and here is what they say.

Slanderers spread fear through their stories, and fear is an evil spirit — God has not given us a spirit of fear, but of power, love and a sound mind (2 Timothy 1:7) [4]. So do not be alarmed by the false and misleading stories; God will cause you to trample over satan and his demonized slanderers, and it is only a matter of time before those slanderers burn in the very fuel they planned to use to burn down your church [4]. David's response is the model: "But I trusted in thee, O Lord: I said, Thou art my God" (Psalm 31:11-14) [4].

Remember too that a slanderer is a devil and an accuser, and one who goes about as a slanderer reveals secrets, while the trustworthy conceals a matter (Proverbs 11:13) [7]. People who fall into sin are to be helped to get up and walk again, not pushed further underground so they never rise again [7]. And God's word stands over His servants: "Touch not mine anointed and do my prophets no harm" (Psalm 105:15) [7].

One caution from the books: correcting the sheep does not mean disgracing them, and if you do not correct, that thing will begin to spread among the congregation [5]. Some need gentleness, and some need to be dismissed, for "Cast out the scorner, and contention shall go out" (Proverbs 22:10) [5].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 5 of *Those Who Are Slanderers* and chapter 11 of *What It Means to Become a Shepherd*.

Scriptures referenced: Psalms 31:11-14; Psalms 105:15; Proverbs 11:13; Proverbs 22:10; 1 Corinthians 5:6-7; 2 Timothy 1:7; Jude 22.

items.question: Why do some Christians who give tithes prosper while others struggle?
items.book: Why Non Tithing Christians Become Poor And Tithing Christians Become Rich
items.text:
The books speak to this directly. Tithing is a seed sown in the house of God, and everyone who sows qualifies for a harvest — "they that sow in tears shall reap in joy" (Psalm 126:5), and "give, and it shall be given unto you; good measure, pressed down, and shaken together, and running over" (Luke 6:38) [3]. Tithing also fulfils the law of humility, since it makes you bow before your Creator and recognise that you did not make it on your own [5][6].

But the books also name reasons tithing does not work for some people. Hidden sin can cancel the blessing, for "he that covereth his sins shall not prosper: but whoso confesseth and forsaketh them shall have mercy" (Proverbs 28:13) [1]. Wrong desires block it, since "ye ask, and receive not, because ye ask amiss, that ye may consume it upon your lusts" (James 4:2-3) [4]. Strife with the brethren hinders it, for "the fruit of righteousness is sown in peace of them that make peace" (James 3:18) [4]. And troubled marriages neutralize prayers, as 1 Peter 3:7 says, "that your prayers be not hindered" [1][4].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapters 14 and 22 of *Why Non Tithing Christians Become Poor And Tithing Christians Become Rich*.

Scriptures referenced: Psalms 75:6-7; Psalms 126:5; Proverbs 28:13; Matthew 6:33; Luke 6:38; James 3:18; James 4:2-3; 1 Peter 3:7.

items.question: A leader I trained for years has just left the church. How do I handle it?
items.text:
I'm sorry — that is a heavy thing to carry, and I want to walk carefully with you here.

First, guard your own heart. The event of someone leaving has an effect on your spirit; leavers pollute you with seeds of hurt, anger, hatred, wickedness and revenge, and you will need to pray long and hard to get free from them, or you will fall into bitterness and unforgiveness [4]. And be careful how you judge the reasons for it — those who derided another church's "bad leader" later had the very thing happen to them, more severely [3].

On the practical side, the books are plain: if anyone indicates his desire to resign, it is best for such a person not to stay but to leave immediately, because his heart has already left the church — "a little leaven leaveneth the whole lump" (1 Corinthians 5:6), and Jesus told Judas, "That thou doest, do quickly" (John 13:27) [7]. Where there is disloyalty, binding such a person is to restrict him; allowing him to operate freely is one of the great mistakes of leaders [2]. And if you have failed to exert your authority, all sorts of people will take you for granted, and weak leaders end up with a far worse crisis [5].

There is also this hope to hold: sometimes the departure of a person heralds the arrival of God's choice for you — it was when Saul's heart departed that David was revealed [6]. And if you are open, each person who leaves you will become a stepping stone to a higher dimension of ministry [5].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 33 of *Victory Secrets*, chapters 1 and 10 of *Those who leave you* and chapter 3 of *Loyalty and Disloyalty*.

Scriptures referenced: 1 Kings 11:3-4; Psalms 141:9-10; Proverbs 3:7; John 13:27; 1 Corinthians 5:6; 1 Corinthians 14:33; 2 Corinthians 7:11.

items.question: How do I forgive someone who hurt me very badly?
items.text:
I'm sorry for the hurt you're carrying. Our books speak to this.

Forgiveness means releasing the hurts, bitterness and wickedness from your heart so that Satan stares in shock at a closed door to your heart [1]. Practically, that means dismissing the thorny, painful issues, giving up all claims against the one who offended you, cancelling any indebtedness, making no more mention of the matter, stopping resentment and anger, and cancelling all punishments you had planned [1][3]. It also means walking in love and praying for your offender, as Jesus said: "Love your enemies... and pray for them which despitefully use you" [1].

One step that makes this easier is to analyse the offender — Jesus prayed, "Father, forgive them; for they know not what they do" (Luke 23:34), because they did not fully know what they were doing [2][5]. Learn to make excuses for people; perhaps your offender is sick, ignorant or confused [5]. Another help is to analyse your own past sins, considering yourself lest you also be tempted [5]. And remember you are equally in need of forgiveness from God, for "if you forgive men their trespasses your heavenly father will also forgive you" (Matthew 6:14) [3].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 18 of *Those Who Are Offended* and chapter 5 of *Forgiveness Made Easy 3rd Edition*.

Scriptures referenced: Matthew 6:14; Luke 23:34; Ephesians 4:32; Hebrews 12:3.

items.question: A member has stopped coming to church and stopped praying. How do I help them come back to God?
items.text:
Our books speak to this. Staying in fellowship matters: if we walk in the light as He is in the light, we have fellowship one with another (1 John 1:7), and if you are in the light you will go to church and fellowship with other Christians [3]. A Christian who doesn't pray is a Christian who will fall into one temptation after another until he eventually backslides, and an uncommitted Christian is a potential backslider [8]. God expects the believer to be like a tree planted by the rivers of water, planted in the house of the Lord, with somebody to relate to as pastor — you need to belong somewhere [8].

So keep the door open and keep praying. It is time to come back home, and staying in fellowship is an important key to receiving the blessings of the Lord [3].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 9 of *How to Pray* and chapter 7 of *Backsliding*.

Scriptures referenced: Psalms 119:133; Proverbs 7:10; 1 John 1:7; 1 John 3:22.

items.question: How can a young person stay away from sexual sin?
items.text:
The books speak to this directly, and I'm glad you asked. First, respect your sexuality rather than denying it — a proper respect for youthful lusts, rather than a denial of them, will save you from them [3]. The will of God is clear that you abstain from sexual immorality (1 Thessalonians 4:3-4), so make it one of your clearest and most energetic goals to practically live a sexually pure life, and stay away from anyone who would want such a relationship with you [2]. Each person keeps himself from fornication differently, so find out what God's will is for your own journey — it may be never reading certain books or watching certain films, never having certain friends, or not working with women or having female secretaries [2].

Practically, the books counsel no untimely relationships — very young people should not enter into courtship, for there is a time for everything (Ecclesiastes 3:1) — and relationships only unto marriage, since the only intimate relationship God approves of is marriage [5]. And do not despair: holiness is engineered by the Spirit of holiness, not by being older, and every young person can be empowered by the Spirit of holiness to become whatever God wants him to become (Romans 1:4) [7]. Young people can live free from sin, for God promises, "I will put my Spirit within you, and cause you to walk in my statutes" [7].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 5 of *The Art of Hearing*, chapters 10 and 13 of *Ready@20* and chapter 4 of *Spiritual Dangers*.

Scriptures referenced: Genesis 3:16; Ecclesiastes 3:1; John 8:46; Romans 1:4; Ephesians 5:5-6; 1 Thessalonians 4:3-4.

items.question: How can my wife and I build a strong marriage?
items.text:
What a good thing to be asking. The books say a happy home does not just happen; it must be developed, and nothing happens by chance [7]. So start with Christ as the foundation and head of your home — when God is the focus of both of you, you draw closer to each other because your closeness to God draws you together, and you end up with a happy home [7]. Build your marriage around the church, and let the Word of God be your manual for marriage [2]. Develop family worship: hold regular quiet times together, or if that is not possible, each of you regularly, but by all means find time once in a while to do it together, especially with the children; attend church services and be involved in church activities, sitting together in church [2][3].

Think as a Christian spouse: do nothing out of selfish ambition or vain conceit, but in humility consider others better than yourselves (Philippians 2:3), reconciling the plans you each held before marriage to suit the home, being willing to give up certain interests and preferences for the sake of the home, and not always insisting on your own way [3]. Be the best of friends, sharing every success, disappointment, joy and pain together, and keep speaking to each other — speaking the truth in love makes you grow up in Christ (Ephesians 4:15) and draws you closer to each other [5]. Choose to speak life, since death and life are in the power of the tongue (Proverbs 18:21): speak good things about your spouse, confess positive things about your marriage, and express your love verbally [5].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapters 7 and 9 of *Model Marriage*.

Scriptures referenced: Job 32:17-20; Psalms 1:1-6; Proverbs 14:4; Proverbs 18:21; Proverbs 24:3; Luke 6:47-48; Ephesians 4:15; Philippians 2:3.

items.question: There is a woman in our church who manipulates and controls people. How do I deal with her?
items.book: Jezebel, A Woman Out Of Order
items.text:
Our books speak directly to this. A Jezebel must not be allowed to operate freely in the church, and it takes the collective rebuke of church leadership to deal with one — one person crying foul will not correct or control her [3][7]. God's word says, "I have a few things against you because you allowed that woman Jezebel" (Revelation 2:20), and if she is left uncorrected you may lose everything, just as Elijah lost his ministry [7].

The mistake many make is wanting to keep their self-respect and not touch the controversial Jezebel, or wanting to maintain good relations with everybody, so they will not rebuke and correct her [7][8]. One man of God confessed that failing to confront the Jezebel in their midst cost him his life, his job, his church and his career — twenty-five years of work [8]. So do not let her operate unchecked; insist on being led by the Holy Spirit and not by any man or woman [2].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapters 4, 17 and 21 of *Jezebel, A Woman Out Of Order* and chapter 15 of *Can’t You Do
Just a Little Bit More?*.

Scriptures referenced: Revelation 2:20.

items.question: What should someone who just gave their life to Christ learn first?
items.text:
What a joy to hear of a new life in Christ. The books say that anyone who comes to Christ will have to be taught the elementary principles of the faith, and that the way you are taught these fundamentals permanently determines your spiritual make-up [2]. So the first thing is to be taught those elementary principles of the oracles of God, as Hebrews 5:12 puts it [2].

It also helps to understand what has happened to you: if you are born again, you have had a spiritual heart transplant, and you need understanding of the concept of salvation so you can grow in grace [7]. And remember the one who led you to Christ, for "in Christ Jesus I have begotten you through the gospel" (1 Corinthians 4:15) — that person is someone never to be forgotten [2].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 8 of *Those Who Forget* and chapter 1 of *Seven Great Principles*.

Scriptures referenced: Matthew 21:34-36; 1 Corinthians 4:15; Hebrews 5:12.

items.question: How should a Christian live simply and avoid wasting money?
items.text:
The books speak to this plainly. A steward will one day be asked to give an account of what was in his control, and if he cannot account for it he loses his position [1]. Wasters tend to become poor, while those who halt the wastage tend to become rich [1]. So cut out waste — most poor nations waste half their resources, and that is why they stay poor [6]. Do not have an expensive lifestyle; cut your coat according to your size, and do not follow bad examples of those who live large on money they owe [6].

Watch your company too, for the prodigal wasted his substance with harlots, and bad company ruins good morals (1 Corinthians 15:33) [3]. And beware the love of money and lust for things, which choke the word and make it unfruitful (Mark 4:19) [5]. There is no short cut: the kingdom is like a mustard seed that must go through the long process of dying and growing [4].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 14 of *He That Hath, To Him Shall Be Given: And He That Hath Not, From Him Shall Be Taken Even That Which He Hath*, chapter 10 of *Opportunities*, chapters 3 and 4 of *How you can become a strong Christian* and chapter 2 of *What it means to be as Wise as a Serpent*.

Scriptures referenced: 1 Samuel 30:3-6; Psalms 27:4; Mark 4:19; Luke 15:12-14; Luke 15:25; Luke 16:1-2; 1 Corinthians 15:33.

items.question: Different topic: how do I pray effectively?
items.text:
Yes, the books speak directly to that. Pray strategic Bible prayers, letting your prayers be guided by the Word of God — for instance Ephesians 1:17-19 and Ephesians 3:15-19 are powerful prayers a minister should pray, and this will make you pray to be grounded in love, which matters because without love you lose your heavenly rewards, as 1 Corinthians 13:3 says [1]. Pray fervently — ardently, with passion and feeling, so that anyone watching could describe your prayer as burning and eager, and you will have great results [2]. Pray in tongues, spending several hours, since Paul said "I thank God that I speak in tongues more than you all" (1 Corinthians 14:18) [2]. And have discussions with the Holy Spirit, because prayer is a two-way affair and you need to hear His voice, as the Comforter "shall teach you all things" [2].

The books also give patterns: pray without ceasing, as 1 Thessalonians 5:17 says, on the bus, in the office, in the shower [3]; pray four times a day — morning, afternoon, evening and all-the-time — since Jesus rose a great while before day and went to a solitary place to pray (Mark 1:35) [5]; enter your closet for effective prayer, because there is a difference between praying alone and praying with a group [5]; and pray for hours about the will of God, as Jesus prayed three times with the same words, which were not vain repetitions (Matthew 6:7) but valuable and effective [7]. There are also short, powerful prayers for crisis moments, as Jesus prayed at Lazarus's tomb (John 11:41,42) [8].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 6 of *Transform Your Pastoral Ministry*, chapters 1 and 7 of *How to Pray* and chapter 2 of *Everything By Prayer 

Nothing Without Prayer*.

Scriptures referenced: Matthew 6:7; Mark 1:35; Luke 6:12-13; John 11:41-42; 1 Corinthians 13:3; 1 Corinthians 14:18; Ephesians 1:17-19; Ephesians 3:15-19; 1 Thessalonians 5:17; James 5:16.

items.question: How can I pray more effectively?
items.text:
Prayer that works is not doodling and dawdling — it is effectual, fervent prayer, and James 5:16 says the effectual fervent prayer of a righteous man avails much [1]. So pray strategic Bible prayers, letting the Word guide you — Ephesians 1:17-19 and Ephesians 3:15-19 are prayers a minister should pray, and praying to be grounded in love matters because without love even great sacrifice profits nothing (1 Corinthians 13:3) [1]. Pray fervently, ardently and with passion, so that anyone watching could describe your prayer as burning and eager [3]. Pray in tongues, as Paul boasted, "I thank God that I speak in tongues more than you all" (1 Corinthians 14:18) [3]. And have discussions with the Holy Spirit, hearing His voice, for the Comforter whom the Father sends teaches you all things (John 14:26) [3].

Make it habitual too — pray without ceasing (1 Thessalonians 5:17), on the bus, in the office, in the shower [4]. Enter your closet alone, for there is a difference between praying alone and in a group, and expanding your ability to pray alone expands what you can achieve in prayer [6]. Watch and pray, staying awake at night, for watching and praying is mentioned more in the Bible than fasting and praying, and Jesus rose a great while before day to pray in a solitary place (Mark 1:35) [8].

items.question: I keep saying hurtful things when I am angry. How do I control my mouth?
items.text:
What you're describing is real, and Scripture takes the tongue seriously: it is "an unruly evil, full of deadly poison" (James 3:8), and no man can tame his tongue on his own — it takes the Holy Spirit to help the believer control it [3]. So the first thing to hold onto is that this isn't a battle you win by sheer willpower.

Practically, the books point to a few things. Anger and wrath are signs of lingering unforgiveness, and we're told to put away bitterness, wrath, anger, clamour and evil speaking, being kind and tenderhearted, forgiving one another even as God for Christ's sake has forgiven us (Ephesians 4:31-32) [5]. And "let not the sun go down upon your wrath" (Ephesians 4:26) — don't let silence or simmering deepen the strain; get the offence off your chest by walking in forgiveness [1]. Also, "neither give place to the devil" (Ephesians 4:27) — give no opportunity to your flesh [6].

One more thing worth sitting with: death and life are in the power of the tongue (Proverbs 18:21), and many Christians have been killed by their own tongues, passing negative comments without knowing the far-reaching effects [7]. Your words are not small things.

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 60 of *Model Marriage*, chapter 1 of *Poison: Taming The Tongue*, chapter 4 of *Forgiveness Made Easy 3rd Edition* and chapter 2 of *Seven Great Principles*.

Scriptures referenced: Proverbs 18:21; 2 Corinthians 10:5; Galatians 5:13; Ephesians 4:26-27; Ephesians 4:29; Ephesians 4:31-32; James 3:8.

items.question: How can I spend time with God every morning without getting bored?
items.book: How You Can Have an Effective Quiet Time with God Every Day
items.text:
What a good question, and our books speak to it warmly. The heart of it is that this time is not a duty to endure but a relationship to enjoy: during quiet time you develop the most important relationship of your life, and a natural relationship develops between any two people who spend quality time together [2]. You draw near to God and He draws near to you, as James 4:8 says [2].

Practically, feed your spirit on the Word rather than trying to manufacture a feeling — desire the sincere milk of the word, that ye may grow thereby, as 1 Peter 2:2 says [1]. A daily dose of the Word increases your faith [7], and a daily quiet time drives away weariness, dejection and depression; the Word is like rain and snow that cools and refreshes, as Isaiah 55:10 says [7]. Vary how you take it in: Bible study and reading in a daily Quiet Time, listening to preaching and church services, since faith cometh by hearing, and hearing by the word of God (Romans 10:17), and praying in tongues, by which you build yourself up in the faith [1]. And remember the habit itself is the point — good habits are difficult to form but easy to live with, and every successful Christian has good habits that brought him to success [3].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 3 of *How to be Born again & Avoid Hell* and chapters 1, 3 and 6 of *How You Can Have an Effective Quiet Time with God Every Day*.

Scriptures referenced: Exodus 3:1-3; Isaiah 55:10; Daniel 6:10; Romans 1:16; Romans 10:17; James 4:8; 1 Peter 2:2.

items.question: And how should I deal with them once I notice it?
items.text:
Our books give several methods, and they are meant to be used together. The first is the teaching method — teaching the Word of God regularly as a preventive process, because teaching fights against deception, and it is only deceived people who go the way of Absalom or Lucifer [5]. The second is the marking and avoiding method: mark those who cause divisions and offences contrary to the doctrine you have learned, and avoid them, for they serve not our Lord Jesus Christ but their own belly, and by good words and fair speeches deceive the hearts of the simple (Romans 16:17, 18) [8]. To mark means to brand or label so the person stands out and can be recognized from afar [8].

The third is dismissal. The books say to dismiss, expel, eject, banish, fire, sack, discard, unseat and lay off any scoffer in your set-up, and that this is the biblical way to deal with disloyal people [4]. This rests on Proverbs 22:10, "Cast out the scorner, and contention shall go out; yea, strife and reproach shall cease" [6]. A leader must refuse to lead people who are mysterious, secretive and questionable in their loyalty, and remove them from the fold, because failure to dismiss them will cause a root of bitterness to grow until many are defiled and the whole church is destroyed [6]. Questionable loyalty is diagnosed when a person makes malicious, damaging or poisonous comments, has a spouse or close relative who is openly disloyal, has friendships and close ties with an openly disloyal person, or is known to communicate with persons who are openly disloyal [6]. Absolute evidence is not needed to deal with mysterious characters — being a mysterious person is deemed enough evidence for dismissal [7].

The fourth is to wipe out the associates of disloyal people. No relationship or friendship with a disloyal person is neutral, so let the friends of your traitors go and join the enemy camp openly [1]. God wiped out Lucifer, and God wiped out the angels associated with Lucifer (Revelation 12:9) [1].

The fifth concerns longstanding workers. It is essential to dismiss disloyal, disobedient, non-compliant or offending bishops, pastors and workers completely from the church, even if they have been longstanding workers, and every reason that merits dismissal must be taken due notice of even if someone has been working for 50 years [7]. But in keeping with the principles of mercy and compassion, financial provisions should always be made for longstanding workers so they can live and work elsewhere without undue hardship, and they should be seen off properly so they live and prosper under a leadership they love and respect [7]. This is based on Paul's warning in Hebrews 12:15 to look diligently lest any root of bitterness springing up trouble you, and thereby many be defiled [7

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 8 of *Now We Are At War*, chapters 7 and 12 of *Those Who Are Ignorant* and chapter 77 of *The Gift Of Governments*.

Scriptures referenced: Proverbs 22:10; Romans 16:17-18; Hebrews 12:15; James 4:4; Revelation 12:9.

items.question: How do I become a better leader of people?
items.text:
What a good thing to want, pastor. The books say plainly that if you are called to the ministry, you are called to leadership, and that good things do not drop on you like ripe mangoes from a tree — you have to study and discover what there is to learn [4]. Decide to be a good minister, as 1 Timothy 4:6 says [4].

To lead is to work on people until they become better human beings, not merely to hold a title [1]. That means reproducing yourself in others so that you are no longer essential, as Jesus prepared His disciples for the day He would no longer be with them (John 16:4,5) [3]. It also means valuing people, because people are the most valuable thing a leader has, and every person who feels undervalued will move away [7]. Practically, that looks like listening to people's problems, letting conversation centre on others rather than yourself, being an encourager, saying thank you, smiling, and not being partial, for the wisdom from above is without partiality (James 3:17) [6]. And wisdom is the master key to the leadership skills you need, for by wisdom kings reign (Proverbs 8:15-16) [5].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapters 2, 20, 23, 86 and 121 of *The Art of Leadership - 3rd Edition* and chapter 4 of *Wisdom Is the Principle Thing For Your Minsitry*.

Scriptures referenced: Ruth 4:15; 1 Samuel 1:8; 2 Samuel 18:3; Proverbs 8:15-16; Proverbs 8:20; Matthew 10:17; Matthew 20:16; John 16:4-5; John 16:16; John 16:23 and 5 more.

items.question: How can they come back?
items.text:
The books describe the way back mainly through repentance and returning to God. Jeremiah constantly urged the people, "Turn away from your wicked ways. Stop doing evil! Repent and come back to God" [2]. God also invites the backslider to reason with Him, saying, "Come now, and let us reason together" (Isaiah 1:18), for He is a rational Being who wants to reason with you [3].

Beyond that, the books point to prayer as the source of strength to stand: Jesus told His disciples to pray because they might fall into temptation, and the author says the Lord gave him strength through prayer [7]. They also stress being planted and committed in a church, since God made us like sheep who need a shepherd and we need to belong somewhere [7]. And they call the believer to adapt to new circumstances rather than turn from God because of them, singing the Lord's song wherever you find yourself, as Psalm 137:4 and Psalm 118:14 say [5].

The books do not lay out a single step-by-step process for restoration beyond these.

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapters 1, 7 and 8 of *Backsliding*.

Scriptures referenced: Psalms 118:14; Psalms 137:4; Proverbs 7:10; Isaiah 1:18.

items.question: How do I deal with disloyal people?
items.text:
Friend, the books speak to this plainly. The first and most important method is teaching: keep teaching the Word of God regularly, because teaching is a preventive work that fights deception, and it is only deceived people who go the way of Absalom or Lucifer [3]. Beyond that, the books say you must be fierce and resolute, not dealing with the enemy in a spirit of benevolence, because disloyalty can end a church or ministry [4].

When it comes to specific people, the counsel is to remove them: cast out the scorner, for Proverbs 22:10 says strife and reproach will cease when the scorner is cast out [5]. Wipe out the associates of disloyal people too, letting them openly join the camp they love, as God cast out Lucifer and the angels associated with him (Revelation 12:9) [1]. Disloyal people are unfit for the work of God and worthless for good work of any kind, so you must protect yourself from them [6]. Handle them God's way, with knowledge and wisdom, binding and restricting a "Judas" rather than letting him operate freely [7]. And dismiss them completely, even longstanding workers, making financial provision so they can live and work elsewhere, to prevent a root of bitterness from spreading, as Hebrews 12:15 warns [8].

items.question: A teenager in our youth group says he cuts himself when he is sad.
items.text:
That is a heavy thing to carry, and I am glad you are walking with him in it. Our books speak directly to this: the madman of Gadara, fully under the influence of Satan, cut himself with stones, and this is described as a very important manifestation of the presence of Satan — self-destruction [8]. Self-destruction is one of the key strategies of demonic attacks; when the spirit of Satan takes hold of a person, he will often begin to cut himself with stones [2]. The demonized man of Gadara tried to kill himself by cutting himself with stones [1].

The books also say that what makes people so sad that they give up on life and become suicidal can only be demons, and that perhaps evil spirits are making a person depressed and sorrowful — with the call to receive deliverance in the name of Jesus [3]. They note too that suicide is a common symptom of depression and can occur in other mental conditions such as schizophrenia and bipolar disorder [5], and that depression is a powerful spirit that can lead people to commit suicide [4].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapters 7 and 14 of *Those who are mad*, chapters 9 and 11 of *Demons and How to Deal with Them* and chapter 2 of *Those who leave you*.

Scriptures referenced: Leviticus 19:16; Isaiah 61:3; Ezekiel 28:16-18; Mark 5:5; John 16:2; Romans 16:17.

items.question: How do I deal with demonic attacks on my family?
items.book: Demons and How to Deal with Them
items.text:
Our books speak to this. Attacks that involve stealing, killing and destruction are caused by the devil and his agents, and spending time to bind demonic powers and destroy their plans will protect you from such evil attacks [1]. When you deal with thieves, murderers and destroyers you are dealing with Satan himself, so deal with the devil in your life by dealing properly with them [1].

Persistent attacks are a sign of demonic activity — Job experienced persistent attacks on his family, his life and his health, and those events were the result of Satan's direct attack on him, as Job 1:12 shows [5]. Demons and demonic activity must be identified in order to be dealt with, so ask God to reveal the real identity of the spirits harassing you [4]. You can also tighten your security: staying with the truth and avoiding deception, practicing righteousness and avoiding sin, and emphasizing salvation all tighten the security of your spirit man against demons, as Ephesians 6:14 says [7].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 18 of *One of You is a Devil*, chapter 20 of *Demons and How to Deal with Them* and chapters 5 and 24 of *Know Your Invisible Enemies*.

Scriptures referenced: Job 1:12; Mark 5:3; Mark 5:5; Luke 8:30; John 10:10; Ephesians 6:14.

items.question: How can I tell when someone in my team is becoming disloyal?
items.text:
Friend, the books say disloyalty doesn't happen overnight — it's a process, and most people don't even notice it in themselves or in those they work with [1]. The first stage is an independent spirit: the person is still part of the church but does what he wants despite contrary instructions, obeying only the instructions he thinks are important [1].

Watch too for the signs: those who absent themselves when the church is going through hard times, since it's in times of pressure that you see a person's true character [2]; inflexibility, where a person is stubborn, unwilling to go beyond what is stipulated, and not prepared to take correction [3]; and assistants who are glad when things go wrong, or who have no comment to make on your suggestions and new ideas, since silence in time of trouble often shows someone not in full agreement [5]. Jesus Himself did not commit Himself to men, because He knew what was in man (John 2:24, 25) [4].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapters 2, 5 and 8 of *Loyalty and Disloyalty* and chapter 7 of *Those Who Are Ignorant*.

Scriptures referenced: John 2:24-25; John 7:3; John 7:5.

items.question: What should I read during it?
items.book: How You Can Have an Effective Quiet Time with God Every Day
items.text:
For what to read, our books say to read a passage from the Bible expecting God to speak to you, praying as Psalm 119:18 says, "Open thou mine eyes, that I may behold wondrous things out of thy law" [5]. You can choose a book of the Bible and read a few verses every day, always remembering where you ended so you continue from the same place the next day — the author had wonderful quiet times reading through Luke and Ephesians in the New Testament, and Genesis and 1st and 2nd Samuel in the Old [5]. Or you can choose a personality from the Bible and follow their life story, a few verses at a time, such as passages about Moses [5].

You may also use a daily Bible reading guide, which is very helpful in developing a regular quiet time habit, and you will benefit from anointed teachers whose ministry helps you grow [4][8]. And when a word or sentence or phrase strikes you, stop there and meditate, turning it over in your mind till the full revelation comes [6].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 3 of *The Secret*, chapter 8 of *Key Facts for New Believers*, chapter 10 of *One Thousand Micro Churches* and chapter 11 of *How You Can Have an Effective Quiet Time with God Every Day*.

Scriptures referenced: Exodus 34:6-8; Psalms 119:18; Ephesians 1:17.

items.question: What does it mean to be a shepherd over a small group of people?
items.book: What It Means to Become a Shepherd
items.text:
Being a shepherd over a small group means you see those people as sheep and relate to them as such [1][4]. A shepherd is a caring, loving guide to the sheep, someone God has called to look after them [3]. That means you have time to care, time to love, time to feed and time to gather the sheep [1].

Your work is to love, care for, guide, teach and feed them [1][6], leading them beside still waters and to green pastures (Psalm 23:2) [5][7], and guiding them even through wilderness situations (Psalm 78:52-54) [7]. It is a great honour to be chosen for this, to have a job in things pertaining to God, and to be expected to have compassion on the ignorant [2].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 1 of *What It Means to Become a Shepherd*, chapters 2 and 3 of *The Privilege* and chapter 20 of *The Art of Shepherding*.

Scriptures referenced: Psalms 23:1-2; Psalms 77:20; Psalms 78:52-54; Psalms 95:6-7; Matthew 9:36; John 21:15-17.
